sentences.text: Chenanisaurus barbaricus is the only known species of this extinct abelisaurid theropod dinosaur, a bipedal carnivore.
Based on measurements of the holotype dentary, this predator measured between 7 and 8 meters in length.
The most striking feature of its jaw is its extreme height relative to its relatively short teeth.
The holotype dentary is missing its posterior end and is damaged in several areas, yet it preserves ten tooth positions including three intact crowns and four broken ones.
The first tooth was small, a trait shared with other ceratosaurs, while the alveoli are rectangular when viewed from above.
Chenanisaurus was estimated to be 7 to 8 meters long, making it one of the largest known abelisaurids.
It is one of the few known African members of the family Abelisauridae.
Researchers explain its short head and high, solid front teeth as a special hunting adaptation where it would strike prey flanks with open jaws to tear off chunks of meat.
The genus Chenanisaurus was named and described by Nicholas Longrich and colleagues in 2017.
The name is derived from the Sidi Chennane mines near Khouribga in northern Morocco where the fossils were first discovered.
The animal is known only from a single holotype consisting of a partial dentary, four teeth, and some isolated attributed teeth, cataloged as OCP DEK-GE 772.
Additional fossils assigned to the genus include two premaxillary teeth and a maxillary tooth found at Sidi Daoui or Sidi Chennane within the phosphate deposits of the Ouled Abdoun Basin.
Chenanisaurus was a predator, like other abelisaurids, utilizing a unique hunting strategy involving open-jaw strikes to the prey's flanks.
The marine location of the fossils suggests the theropod dragged itself into the sea after death, where the holotype fossilized.
Chenanisaurus belongs to the family Abelisauridae and was placed in the basal position of that family, outside the subfamilies Abelisaurinae and Carnotaurinae.

A 2020 analysis by Delcourt and Iori recovered Chenanisaurus as the sister taxon of the unnamed Pourcieux taxon, suggesting it may represent a distinct lineage separate from forms known from the late Cretaceous of South America, India-Madagascar, and Europe.
The genus also belongs to the parent group Etrigansauria.
Chenanisaurus lived during the late Maastrichtian stage of the Cretaceous, approximately one million years before the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Researchers suggest that Morocco may have functioned as an isolated island during the time Chenanisaurus lived.

It is debated whether the enamel wrinkles on Chenanisaurus teeth are unique features or caused by growth anomalies, and whether the genus represents a distinct lineage supporting the hypothesis that Gondwana's fragmentation led to endemic dinosaur faunas.
